https://www.ibtimes.co.uk/barron-trump-a.text: Fresh allegations surrounding Barron Trump have reignited debate over Andrew Tate's connections to influential political circles after a podcast claimed the US President's youngest son privately communicated with Tate and members of his network.According to the host, Barron allegedly took part in meetings, Zoom calls and discussions involving Tate supporters as efforts were made to strengthen the influencer's ties with supporters of Donald Trump.The claims remain unverified, and no evidence has been publicly presented to prove Barron directly assisted Andrew Tate's activities.Claims of Private Contact Come Into FocusThe podcast centred on allegations that Barron Trump developed connections with Andrew Tate and people close to him during Donald Trump's presidential campaign.Citing previous media reports and comments from businessman Justin Waller, the host claimed Barron admired Tate and spoke with him during a private Zoom call last year.According to the allegations, the discussion focused on the criminal proceedings against Andrew and Tristan Tate in Romania. Waller reportedly claimed the conversation included their shared belief that the Romanian investigation was politically motivated.The podcast stressed that Barron allegedly did not discuss helping the Tate brothers legally, but instead talked about wider political issues, including support for Donald Trump's campaign across online platforms.The host argued that these reported conversations suggested Barron had become part of a wider network of conservative influencers rather than remaining a distant observer.As stated during the podcast, 'Barron now 19 admired Andrew and spoke with him over Zoom last year.'Meetings That Allegedly Expanded the NetworkThe programme also revisited earlier reports about Andrew Tate's relationship with members of the Trump family. It claimed Donald Trump Jr reportedly met Tate at Trump Tower in 2017 after the influencer publicly supported Donald Trump online.The host argued these meetings may have helped Tate strengthen his standing among conservative supporters in the United States. He further alleged that several figures connected to Tate later became involved with the Trump political movement, although no evidence was presented to show any formal coordination between them.Attention also turned to an alleged dinner at Mar-a-Lago attended by influencers, where Justin Waller reportedly interacted with Barron Trump.According to the podcast, Waller later described himself as acting like a 'big brother' to Barron and claimed they discussed dating, politics and online influence.The host portrayed these reported meetings as signs that Barron had become familiar with several personalities linked to Tate's growing online community, although none of the participants have publicly confirmed the wider allegations discussed in the episode.Criminal Cases Continue to Shadow Andrew TateMuch of the discussion also revisited the legal controversies surrounding Andrew and Tristan Tate. The host outlined previous allegations investigated by authorities in the United Kingdom and Romania, including accusations involving assault, coercion and human trafficking.The podcast repeated several allegations made against Andrew Tate over the years, while acknowledging that some cases did not result in charges at the time. It also referenced ongoing legal proceedings involving the brothers and argued these investigations continue to shape public opinion about Tate's influence.The presenter suggested that Tate's political relationships became increasingly important as his legal troubles expanded, claiming influential supporters offered public backing while Tate continued denying wrongdoing.

Photograph: Raad Adayleh/AP Jordan Jordan attacks militants in Syria in retaliation for last week’s church attack Jordanian air force says it carried out strikes against ‘terrorist groups’ tied to killing of nine in Karak Associated Press in Amman Mon 26 Oct 2026 18.08 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Jordan has carried out airstrikes against armed groups in Syria in retaliation for Friday’s attack on a Greek Orthodox church in the southern Jordanian city of Karak that killed nine people, the Jordanian air force has said in a statement. It said the operation “resulted in the killing and wounding of many members of these terrorist groups and the destruction of a number of their vehicles”. It did not specify who the groups were or the precise location of the strikes. Syrian state media reported that civilians had been killed in the strikes. The director of health in the southern province of Daraa, where the strikes took place, told the Syrian national news agency, Sana, that at least five civilians had been killed, including women and children and a 65-year-old man. Jordan’s armed forces said the operation was conducted in coordination with Damascus, but Syria’s government gave a contradictory account, saying it had launched an investigation into the ⁠Jordanian attacks, and stressed in a statement the importance of field and security coordination in border areas. Earlier Monday, Jordanian authorities arrested three men for last week’s attack, which also wounded more than two dozen people. The arrests followed a dawn shootout, and all three men were wounded, officials said. The attack struck the Greek Orthodox church during a funeral in Karak, about 55 miles (90km) south of the capital, Amman, on Friday. Karak is home to a minority Christian population. The attack shocked the nation, and Jordan declared three days of mourning for the victims. No group immediately claimed responsibility for the attack; the attackers’ motive remained unknown. Later on Monday, Jordan’t Public Security Directorate identified the three arrested men as brothers Hazzah Zaidan Mohammad and Mishal Zaidan Mohammad, and their brother-in-law Ahmad Sami Hussein. All three are Jordanian; they were taken into custody in Karak, south of Amman. The agency’s chief described the gunmen as “takfiri,” a term used for Sunni militants, but said they were not tied to any organised group. “They only represent themselves,” Maj Gen Obaidallah Abd Rabbo Al-Maayta told a news conference. He also said a large cache of munitions was found in the abandoned house where Jordanian forces apprehended the men. Jordan’s interior minister, Mazen al-Faraya, said the attack by the three men was the result of “a terroristic, extremist way of thinking”. “If this way of thinking is not resolved, we will see incidents like this again,” he told reporters. Jordan’s King Abdullah II had ordered authorities to respond with “an iron fist” against what he called the outlaws of Islam and anyone attempting to undermine the unity of the Jordanian people. “We vowed the terrorists would not escape punishment, and no proponent of dark ideologies that divide Jordanians will be tolerated,” he said in a statement on Monday. Relatives of the victims said the arrests brought them some relief. “Despite the profound and immense tragedy, what happened today has eased our grief, and the grief of the Jordanian people – not just for us, the families of the martyrs,” Khaled al-Borqan, himself a survivor of the attack and a relative of three of the people killed, told Al-Mamlaka. “Despite the sadness and pain, the news brought us joy,” Fares Halaseh, an uncle of one of the victims and a survivor of the attack, told the TV station. But the pain remains, he added. “We will not forget this agony for years to come.” Explore more on these topics Jordan Syria Middle East and north Africa news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness
